facts.statement: Penghusuchus is an extinct genus of gavialid crocodilian.
facts.quote: Penghusuchus is an extinct genus of gavialid crocodylian.

facts.statement: Penghusuchus was a medium-sized crocodilian with an estimated total length of 4.5 meters.
facts.quote: It was a medium-sized gavialid with an estimated total length of 4.5 m.

facts.statement: An excavator driver named Mr. Ming-Kuo Pan discovered a nearly complete skeleton of Penghusuchus on the coast of Neian, Penghu Islands, on March 25, 2006.
facts.quote: On 25 March 2006, on the coast of Neian, Shiyu, Penghu Islands, an excavator driver Mr. Ming-Kuo Pan found a fossilized crocodylian tooth exposed in the sandstone interlayer between basaltic rocks and then dug up a whole skeleton.

facts.statement: The genus name Penghusuchus refers to the Penghu Islands where it was found, while the species name honors its discoverer, Mr. Ming-Kuo Pan.
facts.quote: The genus name is derived from its discovery site in Penghu, and the species name honored its discoverer, Mr. Ming-Kuo Pan.

facts.statement: Fossils of Penghusuchus have been found in Middle to Upper Miocene rocks on Penghu Island, off the coast of Taiwan.
facts.quote: It is known from a skeleton found in Middle to Upper Miocene rocks of Penghu Island, off Taiwan.

facts.statement: Penghusuchus lived during the Tortonian to Messinian stages, approximately 11.63 to 5.333 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Tortonian to Messinian (11.63 to 5.333 million years ago)

facts.statement: Penghusuchus is thought to be related to the fossil Asian gavialids Toyotamaphimeia from Japan and Hanyusuchus from South China.
facts.quote: It may be related to two other fossil Asian gavialids: Toyotamaphimeia machikanensis of Japan and Hanyusuchus sinensis of South China.

facts.statement: Penghusuchus shares mosaic features of both tomistomine and gavialid lineages, potentially filling an evolutionary gap between these two groups of long-snouted crocodilians.
facts.quote: These characters are usually observed in gavialid, suggesting that these two East Asian taxa share mosaic features of both tomistomine and gavialid, filling the evolutionary gap of the two longeirostrine crocodylians.

facts.statement: The presence of a large 7th maxillary tooth is a unique shared feature found in Penghusuchus, Toyotamaphimeia, and Hanyusuchus.
facts.quote: Among these characters, the largest 7th maxillary tooth is only present on Pleistocene Toyotamaphimeia from Japan and Taiwan and the Holocene Hanyusuchus from South China, suggest a unique shared-featured of these three East-Asian taxa.

facts.statement: Penghusuchus is estimated to be smaller than Hanyusuchus and Toyotamaphimeia, with a length of 4.5 to 5 meters compared to the latter two which may exceed 6 meters.
facts.quote: Still, the size of Penghusuchus (4.5–5 m) is estimated smaller than Hanyusuchus and Toyotamaphimeia (may over 6 m), as well as some of the characters is differ from the latter two.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Penghusuchus represents an individual that had reached sexual maturity, indicated by the closure of neurocentral sutures in its precaudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: The holotype of Penghusuchus is an osteological mature individual and reached sexual maturity based on its neurocentral suture in precaudal vertebrae is closed.
